title: a bottle / some water (countable/uncountable 1)
subtitle: a car / cars / some money
summary: Learn the difference between countable nouns (a car, two cars) and uncountable nouns (water, money), and how to use a piece of / a bottle of.

lesson.heading: Countable nouns
lesson.text: You can count these things: one bottle, two bottles, three men, four houses. Countable nouns are, for example: (a) **car**, (a) **man**, (a) **bottle**, (a) **house**, (a) **key**, (an) **idea**, (an) **accident**.

examples.text: There aren't **many cars** in the car park.
We can't get into the house without **a key**.

lesson.note: A singular countable noun never stands alone. It needs **a/an**, **the**, **my** etc.

lesson.heading: Uncountable nouns
lesson.text: You cannot count these things: **water**, **air**, **rice**, **salt**, **plastic**, **money**, **music**, **tennis**. We cannot say ~~one water~~ or ~~two musics~~. Uncountable nouns have only one form: money, the money, my money, some money, much money.

examples.text: There isn't **much money** in the box.

lesson.note: Never use **a/an** with an uncountable noun: ~~a money~~, ~~a music~~, ~~a water~~.

left.label: Countable: a car / cars
left.text: You can count them. Use **a/an** for one, and a plural for more.
examples: There aren't **many cars** in the car park.

right.label: Uncountable: some money
right.text: You cannot count them. There is only one form, and no **a/an**.
examples: There isn't **much money** in the box.

lesson.heading: a piece of ... / a bottle of ...
lesson.note: This is how we count an uncountable noun: *two cups of coffee*, *three pieces of paper*.

lesson.text: Ask yourself: can I say *two ...*? If yes, the noun is countable and one of them needs *a* or *an*.

exercises.prompt: Which words are countable (they take a/an) and which are uncountable?

exercises.explanation: hat is countable, and it begins with a consonant sound.
apple is countable and begins with a vowel sound.
meat is uncountable, so it takes no a/an.
food is uncountable, so it takes no a/an.
I don't need a key. A singular countable noun needs a/an.

exercises.prompt: Match each container or piece with the right noun.

exercises.explanation: music is uncountable, but thing is countable, so we say a wonderful thing.

exercises.prompt: There is a big brown loaf on the table. It's ___ of bread.
exercises.explanation: bread is uncountable, so we count it with a loaf of ... .
coffee is uncountable, so we say a cup of coffee.
Don't go out without an umbrella. umbrella is countable, so it needs an.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
exercises.answer: We can't get into the house without a key.
exercises.explanation: key is a singular countable noun, so it needs a.
